newsitem.title: USA: Army sex case offers something to offend everyone.
newsitem.headline: Army sex case offers something to offend everyone.

text.p: The celebrated sexual misconduct case of Sergeant Major of the Army Gene McKinney offers something to offend practically everyone: African-Americans, women, homosexuals and Army officials.

The pivotal figure in the piece could well be Lt. Col. Robert Jarvis, the presiding officer -- not a judge -- in a preliminary proceeding known as an Article 32 hearing. Jarvis has the unenviable task of deciding whether or not McKinney should face court-martial.

Taking place at Fort McNair, a green oasis in a gray section of Washington's southwest quadrant, the hearing is now in its fifth week. Such hearings typically last several days and most result in a recommendation for court-martial.
But controversial cases, such as McKinney's, often last for months, with the details of the case played out publicly before any trial occurs.
McKinney, a popular 29-year veteran whose post makes him a kind of ombudsman to the Pentagon's top brass on behalf of enlisted soldiers, is accused of sexual misconduct involving five military women.

A decision to send the case to court-martial could rankle African-Americans. McKinney is the first black to be named to this high-profile position, and all five of his accusers are white. He has faulted the Army for racial bias in conducting the investigation and denied all charges.

McKinney's legal team has stressed the informal nature of his office, where non-commissioned officers were on a first-name basis and off-colour speech was accepted. The implication is that women in the office may have gotten the wrong idea, but that no sexual misconduct occurred.

In cross-examining the first and most vocal accuser, former McKinney speechwriter Brenda Hoster, McKinney's lawyers have suggested that Hoster reacted poorly to her boss's criticism of her job performance, and may have sought revenge by alleging sexual harassment.

Hoster, who last year retired from the Army at the rank of sergeant major after 22 years of service, said McKinney made sexual overtures to her on two occasions, in 1995 and 1996, and in the intervening time made comments she judged to be offensive.

She bridled when McKinney's lawyers questioned her memory of specific events after the 1996 incident, calling their inquiry "nit-picking" and asserting her status as a victim. She testified that she felt her former boss would be shielded by a system that favoured rank over justice.

Karen Johnson, vice president of the National Organisation for Women and a former Air Force lieutenant colonel, said in a telephone interview that if the McKinney case does not go to court-martial, it would show "that the military is not really serious about 'zero-tolerance' of sexual harassment."
On another front, suggestions by McKinney's team that Hoster had a lesbian relationship while in the military have disturbed gay rights advocates.

"It is just very disconcerting that the defence attorneys for McKinney would stoop to these diversionary tactics of accusing the accusers as lesbians," said Dixon Osburn of the Servicemembers Legal Defence Network, a watchdog group that monitors the military on gay rights issues.

For Army officials still dealing with the aftermath of widespread charges of sexual harassment by drill sergeants, the McKinney case offers little relief, in part because there is scant scope for face-saving compromise.

To spare everyone the ordeal of a court-martial, Army officials might want to offer McKinney retirement with full benefits. But that is exactly what McKinney has requested, so his accusers might not be satisfied with that deal, and there is little middle ground, according to one Army officer familiar with the process.
